newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Violence erupts as Albanians try to flee port.
newsitem.headline: Violence erupts as Albanians try to flee port.

text.p: Fresh violence erupted at the Albanian port of Durres on Sunday as desperate civilians sought to flee, while U.S. Marines deployed on the beach to evacuate foreign diplomats.
In Tirana, 3,000 Albanians chanting "Peace, peace" gathered in the capital's central square as part of government attempts to restore order.
European Union foreign ministers agreed at a meeting in the Netherlands to send military and police advisers but said they would not mount a military operation to end the violence in Albania.

President Sali Berisha, facing mounting criticism since the collapse of shady investment schemes into which thousands of Albanians had poured their savings, defied demands from southern rebels that he should quit.

Celebratory gunfire erupted in the southern rebel stronghold of Gjirokaster on Saturday night when rumours that Berisha had quit circulated. The guns were fired again, this time in anger, when the resignation was officially denied.
Berisha announced that he had pardoned opposition leader Fatos Nano, who was allowed out of jail earlier this week.
Nano, who had been jailed in 1993 on corruption charges the opposition said were politically motivated, has been mentioned as a possible new leader to unite Albania.
In Durres, 30 km (20 miles) west of Tirana, scores of Albanian police clashed with about a thousand civilians trying to flee the country, witnesses said.
The police beat some civilians and fired hundreds of Kalashnikov rounds over their heads to drive them back from the gates of Albania's largest port.
"We are not killing the people, because they are our brothers, but we have to guard the port," said one policeman.
"The people are coming here because they hope to go to Italy but there is no ship for them."
U.S. marines and Turkish commandos deployed on the beach near Durres to help with the evacuation of some 250 Turkish diplomats and civilians.

The scenes of violence and confusion at evacuation sites and ports contrasted with the calm in Tirana, where the government declared Sunday a day of mourning for the more than 100 people killed, mostly by stray bullets.
An armoured car manned by gun-toting security men patrolled Skanderbeg Square as the crowd clapped the police, waved flowers from the top of a police van and sang patriotic songs.
Some chanted "Hand in the arms," a reference to appeals for gunmen who have been rampaging through Albanian towns to give up their weapons.
Albania's flag, a double-headed black eagle on a red background, flew at half mast by a mounted statue of 15th century national hero Gjergj Kastriot Skanderbeg, who fought the Turks.
Prime Minister Bashkim Fino ordered officials at government offices to report for work on Monday. Many have stayed at home since the unrest erupted.
The government has sought to restore order by parading armoured vehicles and tanks through the streets of Tirana, increasing police pay and appealing for calm.
Unrest erupted across southern Albania in January over the collapse of fraudulent pyramid investment schemes. It spread to most of the country in recent weeks.
At least 20 people have died in Tirana during two days of shooting this week.
The EU, divided over Albania, agreed on Sunday to send military and police advisers in a bid to help restore order.
EU foreign ministers meeting in The Netherlands also agreed to consider providing protection for this mission if necessary, but stressed this was not a military operation.
Meanwhile, the exodus of Albanians across the Adriatic Sea to Italy showed no sign of easing off.
Italian coastguards said they had rescued 858 Albanian refugees from a ship that ran aground off the port of Brindisi.
Another 317 Albanians arrived at the larger Italian port of Bari further to the north on three fishing boats.
Pope John Paul urged Albanians to end "destructive violence" and lay down their arms and said the whole of Europe had a duty to help rebuild the country.
